issues.legal_issue: An allotment may be cancelled in revision when the circumstances justify changing it for equitable resettlement and proper rehabilitation of displaced persons.
material_facts: The allottees had not previously held a temporary allotment in the village and the village was outside the area of the sub-allocation scheme applicable to them.
The competing claimant’s predecessor had held a temporary allotment in the village, and the allotment was shifted because the land had been reserved for a railway project.
The railway project was abandoned, after which the claimant’s heirs sought accommodation in the village.
The Deputy Custodian General considered it equitable and consistent with proper rehabilitation to restore the village land to the claimant’s heirs.
The order cancelling the allotment was made in revision of the Custodian’s rejection of the claimant’s application.
issues.conclusion: The allotment could be cancelled under the applicable Punjab rule because cancellation was equitable and served proper rehabilitation; the Deputy Custodian General’s cancellation was valid.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Punjab rule made pursuant to Sections 55 and 56 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, the Custodian could cancel or vary an allotment where necessary or expedient for equitable distribution under resettlement schemes or for proper rehabilitation of displaced persons (clauses (h) and (i)). The Court accepted that the Deputy Custodian General in revision could exercise the Custodian’s relevant cancellation power.

predicates.revision_of_allotment_decision: A reviewing authority considered, in revision, a decision concerning an allotment.
predicates.original_allotment_outside_allottee_sche: The allottee had no prior temporary holding in the village and the village was outside the applicable resettlement scheme for that allottee.
predicates.competing_claimant_previously_held_villa: The competing claimant or the claimant’s predecessor had previously held land in the village before being moved for a reserved project.
predicates.restoring_claimant_advances_equitable_re: Restoring the claimant to the village would make the distribution of resettlement land equitable in the circumstances.
predicates.restoring_claimant_advances_proper_rehab: Restoring the claimant to the village would advance the proper rehabilitation of displaced persons.

issues.definition: When an allotment is reconsidered in revision and the circumstances show that changing it would advance equitable resettlement or proper rehabilitation, cancellation of the allotment is within the authority of the deciding official.

issues.legal_issue: Certiorari does not permit a reviewing court to correct factual errors or ordinary errors of law in a decision made within jurisdiction; an error of law must be manifest on the face of the record.
material_facts: The allottees sought certiorari under Article 226 to quash the cancellation order.
The asserted errors concerned the interpretation of an application, the approval of the allotment, and the competing claimant’s entitlement to land in the village.
The Court considered those complaints to be factual matters or, at most, ordinary errors of law rather than manifest errors showing ignorance or disregard of law.
The allottees did not establish a jurisdictional defect or a violation of natural justice.
issues.conclusion: The asserted errors did not warrant certiorari, and the Court declined to quash the cancellation order.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226, certiorari is supervisory, not appellate: it may correct jurisdictional errors, unlawful exercise of jurisdiction, violations of natural justice, and manifest errors of law apparent on the face of the record, but it does not permit re-evaluation of findings of fact or correction of a mere wrong decision. The Court relied on Hari Vishnu v. Ahmad Ishaque and T.C. Basappa v. T. Nagappa, and referred to Rex v. Northumberland Compensation Appeal Tribunal; Ex parte Shaw and Batuk K. Vyas v. Surat Borough Municipality.

rule.if: certiorari_petition_against_tribunal_order and tribunal_acted_within_jurisdiction and (challenge_concerns_factual_findings or alleged_legal_error_is_not_manifest) and no_natural_justice_violation

predicates.certiorari_petition_against_tribunal_ord: A party sought a supervisory writ to quash an order made by a tribunal or administrative authority.
predicates.tribunal_acted_within_jurisdiction: The tribunal or authority acted within its jurisdiction in making the challenged order.
predicates.challenge_concerns_factual_findings: The challenge asks the reviewing court to revisit factual findings made by the tribunal or authority.
predicates.alleged_legal_error_is_not_manifest: The alleged error of law is not clear on the face of the record and requires more than identifying a manifest disregard of law.
predicates.no_natural_justice_violation: The party did not establish that the tribunal or authority denied a fair opportunity to be heard or otherwise violated natural justice.

issues.definition: Where a party seeks certiorari against an order made within jurisdiction and the challenge concerns factual findings or a non-manifest legal error, without a natural justice violation, certiorari is not issued.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court should not use a writ proceeding to substitute its choice of which allottee should be displaced when the rehabilitation authorities have exercised their discretion for cogent reasons.
material_facts: The allottees argued that the competing claim could be accommodated by displacing other allottees in the village instead.
The allottees held a larger allotment than the other allottees whose removal they proposed.
The allottees and the other allottees came from the same region, and the allottees’ village allotment had not received the required higher-level sanction described in the departmental instructions.
The Deputy Custodian General gave cogent reasons for not disturbing the other allottees.
The challenge to that choice was brought in a writ proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The Court found no reason to interfere with the rehabilitation authorities’ decision not to displace the other allottees; the dispute was not a proper matter for determination in the writ proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: Certiorari under Article 226 is supervisory rather than appellate and does not authorize the court to substitute its own assessment of an administrative allotment choice where the authorities exercised their discretion for cogent reasons and no prerequisite for certiorari is established. The Court applied the principles stated in Hari Vishnu v. Ahmad Ishaque.

rule.if: writ_challenge_to_allotment_choice and rehabilitation_authorities_exercised_discretion and cogent_reasons_support_selected_allotment and no_certiorari_ground_established

predicates.writ_challenge_to_allotment_choice: A party used a writ proceeding to challenge which of several allottees the rehabilitation authorities selected for displacement.
predicates.rehabilitation_authorities_exercised_dis: The rehabilitation authorities chose how to distribute or retain the available land among competing allottees.
predicates.cogent_reasons_support_selected_allotmen: The authorities gave cogent reasons for retaining the allotment they selected rather than displacing its holder.
predicates.no_certiorari_ground_established: The challenger did not establish a jurisdictional defect, a violation of natural justice, or a manifest error of law.

issues.definition: When rehabilitation authorities make an allotment choice for cogent reasons and no ground for certiorari is established, a court in a writ proceeding does not substitute its own choice.
